metaData.originalTitle: The Case for Physical Media Ownership | Cem Dervis
metaData.title: The Case for Physical Media Ownership | Cem Dervis
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that digital purchases are revocable licenses rather than true ownership, using extensive case studies to show how content can be removed, altered, or lost, making physical media a more reliable choice for preservation, quality, and consumer rights.
metaData.summary: The article builds a comprehensive case for physical media ownership by dissecting the nature of digital transactions. It explains that most 'purchases' are actually revocable licenses, citing legal cases and consumer lawsuits. It then catalogs numerous instances where digital content was removed from users' libraries due to license expirations, service shutdowns, or platform policy changes—including examples from Disney+, HBO Max, PlayStation Store, Nintendo eShop, and Google Stadia. The piece also compares streaming quality (bitrate, compression artifacts, lossy audio) unfavorably to Blu-ray, highlights subscription price hikes, and documents cases of remote deletion (e.g., Amazon's removal of Orwell's *1984*) and post-release alterations (e.g., Disney+ edits to Star Wars). The conclusion is implicit: physical media gives the buyer actual control, resale value, and offline access that digital licenses cannot match.

mainPoints.point: Digital purchases are revocable licenses, not property ownership.
mainPoints.explanation: When you 'buy' a digital movie, game, or book, you typically receive a license that can be revoked if the store loses rights, shuts down, or changes policy. Multiple lawsuits and platform shutdowns prove this.

mainPoints.point: Digital content can be removed or delisted without notice.
mainPoints.explanation: The article documents over a dozen cases where purchased content disappeared: Disney+ removed original films, Sony erased Discovery seasons, and stores like Nintendo eShop shut down, making thousands of games permanently unavailable.

mainPoints.point: Physical media offer superior quality and long-term access.
mainPoints.explanation: Blu-ray delivers 50–128 Mbps video with lossless audio, far exceeding streaming quality. Discs require no account or internet connection, and cannot be remotely altered or deleted.

mainPoints.point: Digital ecosystems can raise prices and restrict usage arbitrarily.
mainPoints.explanation: Streaming subscription costs have increased significantly, while content can be downgraded (e.g., compressed audio) or have features removed. Physical media maintain consistent quality with no recurring fees.

keyQuotes: When a digital store labels a movie, game, or book as a purchase, the transaction is usually a revocable license rather than ownership of the file.
Digital storefronts generally sell access rather than property. If the service or account relationship ends, access to the library can end with it.
A Blu-ray disc, game cartridge, or printed book generally cannot be removed from a shelf by a remote policy change.

relatedArticles.title: Dario Amodei — Policy on the AI Exponential
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Dario Amodei argues that AI is advancing exponentially, creating a dangerous mismatch with slow-moving policy, and proposes concrete actions across regulation, economics, science, civil liberties, and geopolitics to meet the moment.

relatedArticles.title: How to Fine-Tune Nemotron 3.5 ASR for Your Language， Domain， or Accent
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article introduces NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 ASR, a 600M-parameter streaming multilingual speech-to-text model, and provides a detailed, practical guide on how to fine-tune it for specific languages, domains, or accents.

relatedArticles.title: Disney’s New Asia Streaming Boss on K-Drama， Sports and the Untapped Japan Opportunity
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Disney+ Asia Pacific SVP Tony Zameczkowski outlines the streamer's strategy for sustainable growth through local content, sports, and ecosystem integration, with Japan as a key untapped opportunity.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineers detail a five-month experiment building a production software product with zero manually-written code, using Codex agents to achieve 10x velocity and redefining the engineer's role as system designer and feedback loop architect.

relatedArticles.title: Software Architecture Guide
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This page from Martin Fowler presents his perspective on software architecture, defining it as the important stuff in system design, and serves as a curated guide to his site's extensive resources on application and enterprise architecture.

relatedArticles.title: LLM 0.32a0  is a major backwards-compatible refactor
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: LLM 0.32a0 introduces a major backwards-compatible refactor, shifting from a prompt-response model to a message sequence and streaming typed parts abstraction to better handle modern multi-modal LLM capabilities.

relatedArticles.title: Xiaomi MiMo， Explore and Love
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Xiaomi MiMo and TileRT achieve 1000+ tokens/s inference on a 1-trillion-parameter model using commodity GPUs through extreme model-system codesign, including FP4 quantization and DFlash speculative decoding.

relatedArticles.title: Inside FAISS: Billion-Scale Similarity Search
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep, visual, and intuitive explanation of FAISS, covering the core ideas of IVF, Product Quantization, their combination in IVFPQ, and GPU acceleration, to enable billion-scale similarity search.

relatedArticles.title: From Batch to Micro-Batch Streaming: Lessons Learned the Hard Way in a Delta Index Pipeline
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the migration of a batch-oriented delta index pipeline to a micro-batch streaming model, emphasizing that eliminating scheduling delays and adopting deterministic, freshness-driven progress is more valuable than pursuing record-level streaming.
